title: (title unknown)
bodyHtml:
Catio is a language in the Chocoan family spoken by about 15,000 people in Colombia and Panama. Here are some words in Catio, given in no particular order:

1. umé7. kakua ába audu umé
2. kakua ume audu kʰimárẽ8. huwua ába audu umé
3. huwua ũbéa audu kʰimárẽ9. huwua ũbéa
4. huwua ume audu ába10. kakua umé
5. ũbéa11. kakua kʰimárẽ audu ũbéa
6. kakua12. huwua

And here are their English translations, in alphabetical order:

A. eighty-threeG. seven
B. elevenH. three
C. forty-fourI. three hands
D. handJ. twenty-two
E. nineteenK. two
F. personL. two people

C1. Write the letters (A-L) of the English translation corresponding to the Catio words on the answer sheets.

questions.partPrompt: Write the letter (A-L) of the English translation corresponding to each Catio word.

hints.text: Sort the Catio words by shape before you translate anything. Two words appear alone (items 6 and 12), two are pairs of words, and the rest all have the shape (word) (word) audu (word). Notice that only two different words ever stand in first position, and only four different words ever fill the other slots.

This is not a base-ten system. The two words that can start a long expression are body-part or people words that act as multipliers, the four small words that follow them are the numerals one through four, and audu joins the big part of the number to the leftover part, like an English "and". Compare which English translations are large numbers and which are small: the size of the multiplier tells you which is which.

The arithmetic works like this: in a phrase (multiplier word) (numeral) audu (numeral), the value is the multiplier's value times the first numeral, plus the second numeral. So if a multiplier word were worth 5, and the numerals after it were four and three, the whole phrase would come to 5 times 4 plus 3, that is 23. Use the two long phrases that share the same first word to pin down what that first word is worth.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: Group the words by shape

Nothing here is in order, so the first job is to look at the shapes of the Catio expressions rather than their meanings.

  • Single words: umé, ũbéa, kakua, huwua
  • Two words: huwua ũbéa, kakua umé
  • Four words with audu in the middle: items 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 11

In every long expression the first word is either kakua or huwua. The other slots are always filled by one of just four words: ába, umé (also spelled ume without the accent in items 2 and 4), ũbéa, kʰimárẽ. That strongly suggests those four are the small numerals, and that kakua and huwua do a different job.

Step 2: What is audu?

The English side has six plain numbers that are not tiny: seven, eleven, nineteen, twenty-two, forty-four, eighty-three. There are exactly six long expressions. In a lot of the world's languages, big numbers are built as "(some multiple) and (a remainder)". So audu is almost certainly "and" (plus), and the last word of a long expression is the remainder.

Step 3: Find the multipliers

Catio counts by body parts, which is common in the Americas: a hand is 5 fingers and a whole person is 20 fingers and toes. Test that idea. Suppose huwua = hand = 5 and kakua = person = 20, and the numerals are ába = 1, umé = 2, ũbéa = 3, kʰimárẽ = 4.

CatioArithmeticValue
huwua ába audu umé5 x 1 + 27
huwua ume audu ába5 x 2 + 111
huwua ũbéa audu kʰimárẽ5 x 3 + 419
kakua ába audu umé20 x 1 + 222
kakua ume audu kʰimárẽ20 x 2 + 444
kakua kʰimárẽ audu ũbéa20 x 4 + 383

Every one of the six English numbers comes out exactly once, with no leftovers and no clashes. That is the proof that the guess is right: a wrong pair of multipliers would not fit all six numbers at the same time.

Step 4: The short items

Now the leftovers on the English side are: two, three, hand, person, three hands, two people. These match the short Catio items:

  • umé and ũbéa are bare numerals, so they are "two" and "three" - and we already know which is which from the arithmetic above.
  • huwua and kakua on their own are the body-part words themselves: "hand" and "person".
  • A body-part word plus a numeral, with no audu and no remainder, is glossed literally: huwua ũbéa is "three hands" and kakua umé is "two people". (English happens to have separate words for 15 and 40, so the translator chose the literal reading here.)

Step 5: Final matching

ItemCatioAnswer
1uméK. two
2kakua ume audu kʰimárẽC. forty-four
3huwua ũbéa audu kʰimárẽE. nineteen
4huwua ume audu ábaB. eleven
5ũbéaH. three
6kakuaF. person
7kakua ába audu uméJ. twenty-two
8huwua ába audu uméG. seven
9huwua ũbéaI. three hands
10kakua uméL. two people
11kakua kʰimárẽ audu ũbéaA. eighty-three
12huwuaD. hand

The general lesson: many number systems are not base ten. Catio is vigesimal (base twenty) with a five as an intermediate step, and the words for those units are still transparently the words for "hand" and "person".

The solution gives no per-item point breakdown; 20 points were split as 2 points for items 1-8 and 1 point for items 9-12 to total exactly 20 - adjust if an even split is preferred. Note the booklet prints ume without the accent in items 2 and 4 but umé elsewhere; this inconsistency is reproduced as printed. The aspirated k is transcribed with the modifier letter U+02B0 (kʰ), matching the booklet's superscript h. Choices are given as bare letters A-L because the official key is a bare letter; the full option wording appears in bodyHtml.
